note: Behavioural finance simulator (SPEC_V2 §32): one scripted market cycle, six bias-triggering decisions. Values are illustrative arithmetic, not forecasts. The 'planDelta' of each option is the approximate end-value effect in euros, relative to following the written plan, on the stated 100,000 euro portfolio - computed from the scripted path, shown after the run.
setup: You hold a 100,000 euro 60/40 two-fund portfolio. Your written plan: monthly contribution 500 euros, rebalancing band ±5 points, changes only on changed life circumstances.

steps.situation: Year one: markets rally 18 percent. A technology theme fund has tripled; colleagues own it, every feed praises it, inflows are at records.

options.text: Switch 30 percent of the portfolio into the theme fund.
options.bias: herding and FOMO - buying near the top of a chase cycle

options.text: Stay the plan; contributions continue as written.
Stop contributions to wait for a dip to buy the theme cheaper.
options.bias: market timing - the plan already buys every month

steps.debrief: The theme peaked shortly after saturation. Lesson 46: saturated attention and record inflows mark late-cycle herding; the plan's monthly buying needs no opinion.

steps.situation: Months later, a crash: your portfolio falls 25 percent in one quarter. Headlines say 'worst crisis in a generation'. Every login shows red.

options.text: Sell everything; re-enter when things calm down.
options.bias: panic selling - the felt loss made permanent at the bottom, plus a late re-entry

options.text: Hold; contributions continue buying at low prices.
Hold, but stop contributions until recovery is confirmed.
options.bias: loss aversion - 'confirmed' recovery means prices already recovered

steps.debrief: Lesson 44: the sale converts a temporary decline into a permanent loss, and panic sellers re-enter after the easy part of the recovery. The plan's automatic buying is the only reliable 'buy low'.

steps.situation: The crash left your 60/40 at 52/48 - outside the ±5 band. Buying stocks now feels like walking into the fire.

options.text: Rebalance per the band: move bonds into stocks to restore 60/40.
Wait for calm before rebalancing into stocks.
options.bias: loss aversion vetoing the pre-written trade exactly when it is most valuable

options.text: Rebalance the other way - more bonds until the storm passes.
options.bias: panic wearing a discipline costume - it locks the crash allocation in

steps.debrief: Lesson 42: the band rule was written in calm precisely so this trade is compliance, not courage. Executed, it buys the crash on schedule.

steps.situation: Recovery: markets are up 10 percent from the bottom. Commentators call it 'a dead-cat bounce before the real collapse'.

options.text: Sell into strength before the 'real collapse'.
options.bias: recency and narrative - a story about the recent past dressed as a forecast

options.text: Hold the plan; forecasts are not part of it.

steps.debrief: Lesson 46: recency bias extrapolates whatever just happened; lesson 25's evidence - the best days cluster near the worst - makes exit-and-re-enter a systematically losing trade.

steps.situation: Your broker's homepage ranks funds: last year's winner returned +42 percent. Your boring world ETF did +9. Switching takes two clicks.

options.text: Switch the equity sleeve into the ranked winner.
options.bias: performance chasing - buying after the rise, paying for someone else's returns

options.text: Stay: short-run rankings barely persist, and the switch costs spread and tax.

steps.debrief: Lessons 29 and 46: short-run fund performance barely persists, and the investor-return gap is the measured cost of chasing rankings.

steps.situation: An inherited single stock sits beside your portfolio, down 40 percent since you received it. You would not buy it today.

options.text: Keep it until it recovers to its old value, then sell.
options.bias: disposition effect anchored on a price the market has never seen

options.text: Sell and fold the proceeds into the two-fund plan.

steps.debrief: Lesson 44: the loss already exists at market price; 'would I buy it today?' is the only question, and you answered it. Prospects, not purchase prices, allocate money.
